title: Measuring {{term:length}}, {{term:mass}} and {{term:capacity}}
summary: Measure with a ruler, scales and a measuring jug. Estimate first, then measure.
guide: We measure length with a {{term:ruler}}. Always start from the 0 on the ruler, not from its edge.
Each big space on the ruler is one {{term:centimetre}} (cm). Each centimetre has 10 small spaces. Each small space is one {{term:millimetre}} (mm).
We measure mass with scales. When both pans of a balance hold the same mass, the balance is level. 1 {{term:kilogram}} = 1000 {{term:gram}}s.
We measure capacity with a measuring jug. 1 {{term:litre}} = 1000 {{term:millilitre}}s.
Some marks on a scale have no number. First work out what each mark is worth, then count on.
Drag the ruler with your finger, or tap it and move it with the arrow keys.

pencil-from-zero.title: How long is the pencil?
pencil-from-zero.prompt: First estimate: how many {{term:centimetre}}s long is the pencil? Now drag the ruler so its 0 is at the start of the pencil. Write the length.
pencil-from-zero.hint: Put the 0 of the ruler right under the start of the pencil. Then see which number the end of the pencil reaches.
pencil-from-zero.success: Well done! The pencil is 7 cm long.
pencil-from-zero.why: Why must the 0 of the ruler be at the start of the pencil?
pencil-from-zero.model: Because we count from 0. If the pencil does not start at 0, the number at its end is not its length. If the pencil starts at 2 and ends at 9, it is 9 − 2 = 7 cm long.

feedback.not-from-zero: You read the end of the pencil, but the pencil does not start at 0. First drag the ruler so the 0 is under the start of the pencil.
feedback.not-aligned: The 0 of the ruler is not under the start of the pencil yet. Drag the ruler.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Look at the end of the pencil again.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Look at the end of the pencil again.
feedback.empty: Write the length of the pencil as a number.

balance-apples.title: How heavy are the apples?
balance-apples.prompt: First estimate: how many {{term:gram}}s do three apples weigh? Now add weights until the balance is level.
balance-apples.hint: Start with the biggest weight. If the apples' pan is still lower, add a smaller weight.
balance-apples.success: Well done! The balance is level. The apples weigh 600 g: 500 + 100 = 600.
balance-apples.why: How do you know the apples and the weights have the same mass?
balance-apples.model: When both pans hold the same mass, the balance is level. It was level with 500 g and 100 g, so the apples weigh 500 + 100 = 600 g.

feedback.too-big: The weights' pan went down, so the weights are heavier. Take one off.
feedback.too-small: The apples' pan is still lower. Add another weight.
feedback.empty: Put some weights on the balance.

jug-fill.title: 700 ml of water
jug-fill.prompt: The jug only shows 200, 400, 600 and 800. What are the marks in between worth? Now pour in 700 {{term:millilitre}}s.
jug-fill.hint: There is one mark between 600 and 800. That mark is 700.
jug-fill.success: Well done! The water is at the 700 mark.
jug-fill.why: The 700 mark has no number. How did you know it was 700?
jug-fill.model: From 600 to 800 is 200 ml, and one mark sits halfway. So each mark is worth 100 ml, and the mark after 600 is 700.

feedback.too-big: That is too much water. Pour some out.
feedback.too-small: Not enough water yet. Pour in a little more.

dial-rice.title: A bag of rice
dial-rice.prompt: Look at the needle. First estimate: is it more or less than 600 {{term:gram}}s? Now write the mass of the bag in grams.
dial-rice.hint: There is one small mark between 600 and 700, exactly halfway. What is halfway between 600 and 700?
dial-rice.success: Well done! The bag weighs 650 g.
dial-rice.why: What is each small mark on this scale worth? How do you know?
dial-rice.model: From 600 to 700 is 100 g, and one small mark splits it in half. Half of 100 is 50, so each small mark is 50 g and the needle points to 650.

feedback.mark-size: Each small mark is not 1 g or 10 g. Count how many marks there are between 600 and 700.
feedback.rounded: The needle is not exactly on a number. It is between two numbers. Use the small mark.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. The needle has not reached 700.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. The needle is past 600.
feedback.empty: Write the mass of the bag as a number.

leaf-mm.title: Measuring more accurately
leaf-mm.prompt: The leaf is a bit longer than 6 cm. Measure it more accurately in {{term:millimetre}}s. How many millimetres long is the leaf?
leaf-mm.hint: Each centimetre is 10 mm, so 6 cm is 60 mm. Then count the small marks after 6.
leaf-mm.success: Well done! The leaf is 6 cm and 4 mm, which is 64 mm.
leaf-mm.why: Why is 6 cm and 4 mm the same as 64 mm?
leaf-mm.model: Each centimetre is 10 mm, so 6 cm is 60 mm, and 60 + 4 = 64 mm. Millimetres are smaller than centimetres, so the measurement is more accurate.

feedback.wrote-cm: That is the number of centimetres. We asked for millimetres. Each centimetre is 10 mm.
feedback.nearest-cm: That is the length to the nearest centimetre. Be more accurate: count the small marks after 6 too.
feedback.reversed: The digits are swapped. Centimetres first: 6 cm is 60 mm.
feedback.not-from-zero: The leaf does not start at 0. Move the ruler back so the 0 is under the start of the leaf.
feedback.not-aligned: The 0 of the ruler is not under the start of the leaf. Move the ruler back.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Count the small marks again.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Count the small marks again.
feedback.empty: Write the length of the leaf in millimetres.
